strengths: The paper targets an important bottleneck: exact autoregressive decoding for long-convolution sequence models, and clearly distinguishes prompt-based and online generation settings.

The prompt-decoding decomposition is simple and potentially useful: one FFT summarizes the prompt's contribution to future outputs, after which only contributions from newly generated tokens are computed.
The manuscript provides concise asymptotic analyses and attempts to connect the method to several relevant model families, including STUs, Hyena, and long-convolution architectures.
The synthetic CPU experiment qualitatively exhibits the expected sublinear amortized scaling.
weaknesses: Algorithm 2 appears incorrect as written. The cache is uninitialized at the first iteration, and after a refresh its definition includes u_t while the prediction separately includes u_t, creating an indexing/double-counting error. Consequently, Lemma 2's runtime analysis does not establish a correct generation algorithm.

Algorithm 3 inherits the cache-indexing problem and also reads C_0 on its first iteration. Moreover, its update M^{t+1}=∇ℓ_t(M^t) is not a standard online-gradient update. The assertion that it preserves the original spectral-filtering regret bound is therefore unsupported; no formal regret theorem or proof is provided.

The empirical evaluation is far below top-tier standards: it contains only a single-layer synthetic CPU timing study, with no real model or task, GPU measurements, prompt-prefill experiment, memory measurements, correctness-error verification, optimized block-convolution baseline, ablations, variability estimates, or sufficient implementation and hardware details for reproducibility.
The text makes unsupported practical claims about observing gains on large accelerated models despite presenting no corresponding results.

Novelty is insufficiently established relative to classical FFT block-convolution techniques such as overlap-add/overlap-save. The core idea resembles standard batching of future convolution outputs, but these connections and distinctions are not discussed.

The scope claims are too broad. Applicability to arbitrary convolutional models, including multilayer architectures with nonlinearities and data-dependent gating, is asserted without an algorithm, complexity analysis, or experiment demonstrating end-to-end exact decoding.

The notation and problem definition are inconsistent about whether L is the model's fixed convolution context, the prompt length, or the total horizon. Algorithm 1 requests a filter of length L+K despite defining the model's filter length as L, and the baseline runtime expressions are not adequately justified under a consistent convention.

Important complexity factors such as channel dimensions, number of filters, layers, nonlinear operations, and FFT/cache-management overhead are suppressed, limiting the relevance of the theoretical comparison to actual sequence models.

strengths: The core decomposition is simple and useful: FFT-precompute the contribution of a known history block, then evaluate only the within-block contribution during decoding. For a single linear convolution, this appears exact and yields a genuine time-memory tradeoff. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_iclr2026_yao_medium_20260919T2254Z/scratch/e7f1a2789d11455190b02e0937543e78/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The paper is concise, and the intuition behind FutureFill is relatively easy to follow.
The stated prefill bound, O(L log L + K^2) time with O(K) cached values, could be useful when K is much smaller than L.
The attempt to connect the technique to spectral filtering and preserve exact predictions, rather than introduce an approximation, is potentially valuable.
weaknesses: The novelty is inadequately established. FutureFill is essentially blockwise or partitioned FFT convolution, yet the paper does not discuss classical streaming/online convolution, overlap-add/overlap-save, partitioned convolution, or stronger online-convolution algorithms. Consequently, the claim that O(KL) is the best-known exact baseline is not convincing, and the comparison is largely against a naive implementation.

The experimental evidence is far below top-tier standards. It consists of one single-layer CPU timing exercise on an unspecified synthetic convolution, with only a few sequence lengths and fitted asymptotic curves. There are no real models or tasks, GPU measurements, optimized baselines, memory measurements, numerical-error checks, output-quality checks, variance estimates, or experiments for the prominently claimed prompt-prefill setting.

The experiments are not reproducible: the manuscript gives no hardware specification, implementation details, dimensionalities, kernel configuration, number of repetitions, error bars, or code. The statement that gains were observed for large models on accelerated hardware is anecdotal and unsupported.

The formal specification contains consequential inconsistencies. The model is defined with a filter in R^L, whereas Algorithm 1 requires a filter in R^(L+K); L alternates between context length and total online horizon; and some convolution lengths and indexing conventions are unclear. These issues make it difficult to determine precisely which fixed-context model the theorems cover.

Algorithm 2 uses C_tau before the cache has ever been initialized: tau starts at 1, while cache construction occurs only when tau > K. Algorithm 3 initializes the cache, but its stated learning update assigns the parameters to the gradient rather than performing a gradient step or projection. These are not merely presentation details in algorithms used to support exactness and regret claims.

The corollary asserting the same spectral-filtering regret bound is given without a theorem statement, assumptions, or proof. While exact feature computation may make such a transfer plausible, the actual learning algorithm and its update are not specified correctly enough to establish it.

The broad claim that the method applies to any convolutional model is not substantiated. The analysis treats essentially a scalar linear convolution and hides channel width, kernel multiplicity, depth, nonlinearities, gating, and data-dependent operations. Mentioning Hyena and STU is not a substitute for deriving the multilayer complexity or demonstrating an implementation.

The baseline tables omit relevant alternatives and important costs. They suppress feature dimensions and model depth, compare against naive convolution and attention formulations, and do not analyze FFT constants, cache-construction latency, numerical precision, or optimized recurrent realizations available for structured kernels.

Overall, the underlying algebraic trick is plausible, but the missing positioning, algorithmic inconsistencies, unsupported generality, and extremely limited evaluation prevent the central novelty and practical-impact claims from being established. This is substantially below the acceptance threshold rather than a borderline submission.

strengths: FutureFill presents a simple and potentially useful idea: summarize a prompt's contribution to future convolution outputs with one FFT, then compute only the contribution from newly generated tokens. Algorithm 1 plausibly provides exact generation in O((L+K) log(L+K)+K^2) time with O(K) persistent cache.
The distinction between prompt-based and online generation is helpful, and the paper clearly communicates the intended time–memory tradeoff.
The method is model-agnostic at the level of causal convolutions and could potentially be incorporated into architectures such as STU, LongConv, and convolutional components of Hyena.
The synthetic timing experiment qualitatively exhibits the predicted sublinear amortized scaling.
weaknesses: Algorithm 2 appears incorrect as written. When the cache is refreshed at time t, C_j is constructed for a future prediction at t+j, but tau is reset to 1 and C_1 is used immediately for the prediction at t. For example, C_1 includes phi_2 u_t, whereas the desired current convolution contains phi_2 u_{t-1}. The initial cache is also not initialized before its first use. Consequently, Lemma 2 and the online experimental result are not established by the stated algorithm.

The STU case study inherits the online-algorithm issue and contains an invalid-looking learning update, M^{t+1}=∇ell_t(M^t), rather than a specified online optimization step. No actual regret theorem, assumptions, or proof is supplied to justify the claim that the original regret guarantee is preserved.

The evaluation is far below the standard needed to substantiate practical relevance: it contains only a synthetic, single-layer CPU timing test, with no task accuracy, real model, GPU benchmark, strong implementation baseline, memory measurement, ablation, numerical-correctness test, hardware details, repetitions, or error bars. The assertion that gains materialize in large accelerated models is anecdotal.

Novelty and positioning are insufficiently established. The method is essentially blockwise FFT evaluation of an online convolution, but the paper does not compare against classical partitioned, overlap-based, relaxed, or online convolution algorithms. It therefore neither demonstrates that the square-root tradeoff is new nor explains why more sophisticated online convolution schemes are inapplicable.

The definitions and headline claims are inconsistent about context length: Algorithm 1 requires a filter of length L+K even though L is repeatedly called the model context length. Simplifying the FFT term to O(L log L) also requires the K≤L assumption to be stated formally.

Complexity accounting suppresses important factors such as channels, layers, nonlinear architecture structure, FFT workspace, and hardware efficiency. The comparison table also omits the K^2 decoding term for standard attention while including it elsewhere, weakening the fairness of the comparison.

Overall, the prompt-caching result is promising but elementary, while the online result has a concrete correctness problem and the empirical evidence is too limited. These issues prevent the submission from being competitive at a top-tier AI conference in its current form.

strengths: The paper addresses an important inference bottleneck and presents a simple, broadly applicable FutureFill primitive for exact autoregressive decoding with fixed convolutional operators.

The Continuous-FutureFill algorithm improves the total decoding complexity from quadratic to O(L log^2 L), while the epoched variant exposes a useful compute-memory trade-off. The prompt-generation extension also yields an attractive cache size that depends on the generation length rather than the prompt length.

The main algorithmic intuition is clear, and the divide-and-conquer interpretation makes the online convolution construction relatively accessible. Deferred proofs substantiate the core correctness and runtime claims, notwithstanding some notation issues.

The evaluation covers controlled scaling experiments, prompt and no-prompt settings, multiple model widths and depths, hybrid convolution/attention models, long sequences, and models up to roughly 826M parameters on an H100.

The realistic-model results demonstrate meaningful gains at long contexts, including approximately 1.7x speedup without prefill and roughly 2x in the reported long-prompt setting. The cache-length sweep also agrees with the predicted optimum.
The method is mathematically exact rather than relying on model distillation or an approximation of the convolutional model, and the paper appropriately acknowledges closely related concurrent work.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited by concurrent Flash Inference work, which already obtains the same O(L log^2 L) online-convolution complexity using relaxed polynomial interpolation. The primary differentiation is therefore the simpler formulation, the epoched variant, and prompt-cache analysis rather than the headline asymptotic result.

The claimed O(K) total additional memory for Epoched-FutureFill is not adequately justified. Algorithm 1 repeatedly computes a FutureFill involving prefixes of length up to L, and the stated standard FFT computation ordinarily requires O(L) temporary workspace. A blocked/truncated FFT implementation might recover a smaller workspace bound, but neither such an algorithm nor its complexity proof is supplied. Similar care is needed to distinguish retained O(K) prompt cache from peak prefill workspace.

The strongest asymptotic method, Continuous-FutureFill, is tested only in the small controlled experiment and is not evaluated on the realistic deep models. Those experiments instead use the asymptotically weaker epoched algorithm, leaving the practical value of the headline O(L log^2 L) result unclear.

The empirical comparison is narrow: the realistic experiments compare only against naive online convolution. There is no practical comparison with the closely related Flash Inference method, recurrent realizations where available, or other optimized exact convolution implementations. The Transformer comparison uses a tiny two-layer, width-32 setup and is not especially informative.

The language-model experiments use randomly initialized convolutional filters and evaluate only runtime. Exactness makes task quality less central, but the paper should still report numerical agreement with naive decoding, since FFT roundoff can compound during autoregressive generation, especially across very long sequences and mixed-precision models.

Experimental uncertainty is estimated from only two post-warmup measurements. Several reported speedups emerge only at extremely long sequences, while FutureFill is slower than the baseline at shorter lengths; throughput, peak memory, kernel-level profiling, and crossover points should be characterized more carefully.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the manuscript says the FlashSTU source is publicly available but displays no repository URL for it or the proposed implementation. Important implementation details are present, but code, exact configurations, and a direct correctness test are missing.

There are multiple technical presentation defects, including an undefined k(t) for odd t under the paper's definition of [b], indexing/range inconsistencies around FutureFill and Algorithm 3, failure to specify truncation of out-of-range cache updates, and typographical errors in tables and prose. These appear repairable but reduce confidence in a proof-heavy submission.

Overall, the core idea is promising and largely credible, but the overlap with concurrent work, insufficient support for the low-memory claim, limited baselines, and lack of realistic evaluation of the main algorithm place the submission marginally below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: FutureFill is a simple and intuitive primitive, and the paper clearly explains how it enables exact online convolution without approximation.
The quasilinear O(L log^2 L) runtime result is meaningful for convolutional models that lack an efficient recurrent representation.
The paper evaluates both prompt-free and prompted generation over long sequences and several model sizes, with results showing eventual speedups over naive convolution.
weaknesses: The principal O(L log^2 L) result has limited novelty: the paper acknowledges concurrent work achieving the same complexity, while the distinguishing memory/runtime trade-off is not established convincingly enough to compensate.

The low-memory theorem appears to omit substantial working storage. Algorithm 1 repeatedly computes FutureFill from the entire prefix u_1:t, requiring that prefix and ordinarily O(t)-scale FFT workspace. The claimed O(K) total additional memory is therefore unsupported unless a nonstandard storage and FFT model is specified and analyzed. This also weakens the headline cache claims.

The practical evaluation uses randomly initialized convolutional filters rather than trained language models. It establishes execution-time behavior but does not demonstrate realistic generation, numerical agreement under autoregressive error accumulation, or usefulness on an actual sequence-modeling task.

The only serious implementation baseline is naive online convolution. There is no empirical comparison with the concurrent quasilinear algorithm, optimized exact alternatives, recurrent realizations where available, or distillation-based approaches. Consequently, the reported speedups do not establish competitiveness with the state of the art.

The practically evaluated Epoched-FutureFill method is frequently slower at short and moderate lengths and reaches only about 1.5–1.7x speedup without prefill at extremely long generations. Continuous-FutureFill, which supplies the strongest asymptotic result, is not evaluated on the deep models.

Experimental reliability and reproducibility are weak: results come from one accelerator, means and standard deviations use only two post-warmup measurements, memory consumption is not reported despite being a central claim, and no usable implementation link is provided in the manuscript.

There are specification and presentation defects in the technical material. For example, Algorithm 2 leaves k(t) undefined for odd t because its defining set excludes zero, although the proof later assumes k=0; several claims also blur persistent cache size, peak working memory, and storage of past activations.

The claim of applicability to “any convolutional model” is broader than the evidence. The analysis treats fixed linear convolutions, whereas practical architectures may include multiple channels, gating, nonlinear blocks, input-dependent operations, finite precision, and quantization; these extensions receive little formal or empirical validation.

strengths: The manuscript presents a meaningful exact-inference contribution: FutureFill reduces online convolution from quadratic to O(L log² L) time, while prompt-conditioned generation takes O(L log L + K log² K) time with an O(K) persistent cache. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_iclr2026_yao_medium_20260919T2254Z/scratch/3ede9e53defd41a49b0939b3efb95a36/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The FutureFill primitive is simple, broadly applicable to convolutional sequence models, and supported by correctness and runtime analyses. The epoched variant adds a useful compute-memory tradeoff and is more practically distinctive than the continuous variant.

The evaluation covers synthetic scaling tests and large convolutional and hybrid models on an H100, with variations in generation length, prompt length, model depth, width, and cache size. The observed subquadratic scaling and roughly 1.5–2× gains at long contexts support practical relevance.
The paper clearly distinguishes exact generation from approximation-based acceleration and candidly acknowledges concurrent work that obtains the same asymptotic runtime.
The presentation is generally clear, and the appendices contain detailed proofs, implementation information, and extensive timing tables.
weaknesses: The claimed O(sqrt(L log L)) total additional-memory bound for Epoched-FutureFill is not convincingly established. Each cache refresh invokes an FFT-based FutureFill over sequences of length O(L), whose ordinary implementation requires O(L) working storage. The paper appears to count the retained cache but not transient FFT workspace; indeed, the described implementation pads and transforms full-length arrays. This distinction should be formalized, and either a genuinely space-efficient construction or a peak-memory qualification is needed.

Novelty is reduced by concurrent work [24], which achieves the same O(L log² L) online-inference complexity. The epoched tradeoff and simpler formulation remain useful contributions, but the paper does not experimentally compare against that method.

The deep-model experiments use randomly initialized filters rather than trained language models. This is adequate for measuring kernel scaling but does not fully establish benefits under realistic trained activations, decoding behavior, batching, or production inference settings.

Although the method is algebraically exact, FFT execution in float32 is not numerically exact. The paper reports no output-error, logit-error, or token-agreement measurements against naive convolution, leaving an important practical interpretation of its central exactness claim untested.

Full-model experiments benchmark only Epoched-FutureFill against naive convolution; Continuous-FutureFill, the method supporting the strongest runtime theorem, is not evaluated on the large models. Comparisons to optimized recurrent/SSM implementations or other exact convolution-inference approaches are also absent.

Timing uncertainty is weakly characterized because reported means and standard deviations use only two post-warmup runs. Moreover, FutureFill can be slower at shorter lengths, so the practical win is concentrated in unusually long generations.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the manuscript's purported FlashSTU source-code URL is blank, and no dedicated FutureFill implementation link is visible. There are also minor algorithmic specification issues, such as the undefined k(t) for odd t under the stated index set and unqualified cache updates beyond the sequence boundary.
